passage: The computer lab smelled of dust and warm plastic. Zubin had thirty minutes before the science project was due and a blank page. "Just this once," he told himself, opening Vijay's file from the shared folder and retyping the paragraphs in his own order. Half the class had done the same last term. He handed it in and felt sick for an hour. On Friday the teacher put both projects on the desk and asked quietly, "Zubin, can you tell me how you reached this conclusion?" He could not explain the second graph. The teacher gave him a fresh topic and three days. Zubin stayed back in the library and, slowly, made the graph himself.

qa.q: How long did Zubin have before the project was due?
qa.a: Zubin had thirty minutes before the project was due.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling after handing the project in?
qa.a: Sick with guilt for an hour, despite telling himself it was just this once.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Zubin?
qa.a: When the teacher asked a calm question and he could not explain the graph, he accepted a fresh topic and stayed back to make the graph himself.

qa.q: How might the teacher see the two similar projects?
qa.a: As a sign that a student may be struggling or under pressure, so the teacher asked a calm question and did not punish at once.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who copies work under deadline pressure, tells himself it is just once and cannot explain it later.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,
Last night I finally understood why I am scared of Thursday's test. For three weeks I have been copying the algebra homework from a solutions site an hour before it is due, telling myself it is only for tonight. Everyone in our class does it, so it felt normal. My homework marks are perfect. In class yesterday, Ms Thomas put a similar problem on the board and I froze. I have the copied pages, but nothing in my head. Tonight I opened a fresh notebook and did the first two problems myself, slowly and badly, but they are mine. I am going to ask Ms Thomas for help on Monday. Write back and tell me if you have ever felt this.
Joseph

qa.q: How long before the deadline did Joseph copy the algebra homework?
qa.a: Joseph copied it an hour before it was due.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the similar problem was put on the board?
qa.a: Frightened and exposed, since the copied pages left nothing Joseph could use.

qa.q: What could Joseph do on Monday and after?
qa.a: Ask Ms Thomas for help and keep solving problems independently, even slowly.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, but trusted with an honest confession, and likely supportive.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who copies homework each night as a common habit and finds that it weakens the ability to do the work.

passage:
Yash, your cousin says you copied the science project from a website. Sit. Let your Kishore dada tell you about Class Nine.
Our geography map-work was due on Monday. I had played cricket all weekend. On Sunday night, I copied my friend Dinesh's whole file, even his mistakes. I told myself, "Just this once. Everyone does it."
The teacher didn't catch it. I felt clever for a week.
Then it happened again for history. And again for maths homework. Each time, "just this once." By Class Ten, I couldn't read a map on my own. In the board exam, there was a map question worth eight marks. I sat looking at it, and my hand was sweating. I knew I had never actually learned it.
I got two marks out of eight. Dinesh got all eight, from his own work.
I'm not angry with you, beta. I'm telling you because "just this once" is how it starts.

qa.q: How many marks was the map question worth?
qa.a: Eight marks.

qa.q: How did young Kishore feel in the board exam, looking at the map question?
qa.a: Kishore felt panicked and ashamed, hand sweating, knowing the skill had never been learned.

qa.q: At what point in the story could a different choice have changed things?
qa.a: On that Sunday night in Class Nine, doing the map-work himself, even late and imperfect, instead of copying Dinesh's file.

qa.q: How might Dinesh have felt if he had known about the copying?
qa.a: Dinesh might have felt used and annoyed, since his own work, mistakes and all, was taken without asking.

grounding: An elder recalls copying under deadline pressure, telling himself it was just this once, until the habit eroded his own ability.

passage:
At 11 p.m. the power went out. Pradeep's physics assignment was due at eight the next morning, and he was only on question three of ten. His phone battery was at twelve percent.
Then a message from his classmate Sarika in the group: photos of her finished answers. "For anyone stuck 🙂"
Pradeep hesitated. His father had said if his marks dropped again, no more cricket academy. Everyone in the group was probably copying anyway. Just this once.
He copied all seven by torchlight, changing a few words. He felt a small knot in his stomach, but mostly relief. He slept at midnight.
He got nine out of ten.
Two weeks later, the unit test had the same kind of questions. Pradeep stared at the paper. He recognised the questions but not the steps. He had written them, but never done them.
He scored eleven out of thirty. Sarika scored twenty-seven.

qa.q: What was Pradeep's phone battery at?
qa.a: His phone battery was at twelve percent.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he copied by torchlight?
qa.a: Pradeep felt a small knot of guilt in his stomach, but mostly relief at escaping the deadline.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Pradeep have done instead?
qa.a: Copying got the marks but not the skill, so the test showed the gap; he could have done fewer questions honestly or asked the teacher for more time.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel if she learned her answers were copied?
qa.a: Sarika might feel uneasy, since Sarika meant to help people who were stuck, not to have her work copied whole.

grounding: Shows a teenager who copies an assignment under deadline pressure, telling himself it's just this once, and finds his own ability eroding.

passage:
In their school in Kothrud, lab records were due every Friday. Jeevan had fallen three weeks behind.
On Thursday afternoon, Kiran handed him her record book in the library. "Copy what you need. Everyone does."
Jeevan looked around. Two other boys were doing the same thing at the next table. It felt normal. Just this once, he told himself, to catch up. He copied three experiments in forty minutes, readings and all.
His record was stamped "Complete" on Friday. For a moment he felt clever.
Then, in the practical exam in March, the examiner asked him to set up the pendulum experiment and explain why the readings changed. Jeevan had written about it three times. He had never done it. He stood with the string in his hand and his face burning.
Kiran, at the next bench, finished in ten minutes.
Walking out, Jeevan thought: I didn't catch up. I just moved the problem to March.

qa.q: How many experiments did Jeevan copy?
qa.a: He copied three experiments in forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel standing with the pendulum string in the practical exam?
qa.a: Jeevan felt exposed and ashamed, face burning, because he had written about the experiment but never done it.

qa.q: What lesson does Jeevan draw, and how could he act on it?
qa.a: That copying only moved the problem later; he could ask the teacher for extra time to do the missed experiments himself.

qa.q: How might Kiran see her offer to share the record book?
qa.a: Kiran probably thought she was being helpful and that everyone did it, without realising it could leave Jeevan unprepared.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who copies lab records to meet a deadline, calling it normal, and later finds he cannot do the work himself.

passage:
"Naveen, please. Just send me photos of your practical file. Just this once."
"It's due at eight tomorrow, Preeti. You said you'd started."
"I had tuition, then the maths test, then Mummy's cousin came over... I've done two experiments out of ten."
"Everyone copies the practical file anyway."
"Exactly! So it's not a big deal."
Naveen hesitated, then sent the photos. "Change the readings a bit at least."
At one in the morning Preeti was writing "the solution turned pale pink" for an experiment she had never seen. She paused. Last term she had copied the physics file too, and in the viva she couldn't explain a single diagram.
"Ma'am will ask questions in the viva," she typed.
"Then just learn my answers," Naveen replied.
Preeti looked at the page, then at the empty titration columns. She kept copying, but slowly, and her stomach stayed tight the whole time.

qa.q: How many experiments had Preeti done?
qa.a: Two experiments out of ten.

qa.q: What does Preeti's tight stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Preeti feels guilty and uneasy, remembering the viva where she couldn't explain the copied physics file, even while telling herself it is just this once.

qa.q: What could Preeti do instead of copying tonight?
qa.a: Preeti could write up the two experiments honestly and tell the teacher in the morning that the rest is late, asking for a short extension.

qa.q: What is it like for Naveen when Preeti keeps asking?
qa.a: Naveen seems torn, hesitating before sending the photos and then trying to limit it with "Change the readings a bit at least."

grounding: Shows a teenager copying work under deadline pressure, telling themselves it is just this once while their own ability slips.
